2017_109_062017mtg.paragraph: Agenda packet for the Troy Board of Education regular meeting of June 20, 2017 at the Services Building — the year-end meeting, and the largest packet of 2017. It opens with a public hearing on the 2017-2018 budget and adopts appropriations of $147,430,144 for the General Fund at 18 mills non-homestead. It ratifies the TEA contract running July 1, 2017 through January 31, 2020; authorizes the sale of 18 acres in Section 11 to Mondrian Properties, L.L.C. for $4,225,000.00; adopts $419,606.82 of world language and $171,735.32 of ELD materials; renews the First Student, Safe-Ed, Clean-Ed and Sodexo contracts; switches workers' compensation to full coverage at not more than $98,968.00; and receives the Epic MRA sinking fund survey showing 61% outright Yes on a 1-mill proposal.

**Meeting**
Regular meeting, June 20, 2017, 7:00 PM, Services Building, 4420 Livernois. The agenda opens with business rather than recognition, because item 2.A is a **public hearing on the preliminary 2017-2018 budget**.

**Recognition**
Dr. Machesky introduces the "2016-2017 School Year in Review" video. The Mission Moment features Athens' **AP Capstone program**: AP Seminar teachers Brenda Rice and Sue Syme and AP Research teacher Rachel Webb present, followed by a question-and-answer session in which the students themselves field Board questions about the program — chosen, the item says, "based on their success in the program and their ability to express themselves well."

**Consent agenda**
Treasurer's Report for April and May 2017.

**Personnel — the teacher contract**
A tentative agreement between the Board and the Troy Education Association/MEA/NEA was reached **June 9, 2017**, signed by TEA president Tony Lucchi and Assistant Superintendent Jordan Harris, and **ratified by the TEA membership June 16**. The contract runs **July 1, 2017 through January 31, 2020**. The bargaining team the Board appointed in February — Harris as chief spokesperson with West, Dziatczak, Griffor, Trotter and Pass — closed it eleven days before the old agreement expired.

**David Recker** is appointed Assistant Principal, Larson Middle School, effective July 1, 2017, on a two-year probationary contract. He began teaching language arts and journalism at Dayton Early College Academy in 2012, moved to Troy in 2014 to teach language arts at Troy High, implemented ISTE standards, led the Continuous Improvement Committee and coordinated several clubs; he holds a bachelor's from the University of Dayton and an M.A. in K-12 education administration from Michigan State.

**Curriculum — two adoptions**
Secondary world language materials for grades 6-12 covering **Chinese, French, German, Japanese and Spanish**, presented by Mark Dziatczak and Jennifer Gottlieb, at **$419,606.82**. ELD materials for grades 6-12, presented by Dziatczak and Christin Silagy, at **$171,735.32**. Board members reviewed the textbooks and discussed both at the June 13 workshop.

**Business — the budget**
The 2016-17 budget amendment sets the General Fund at **$146,020,168**, Capital Projects at $16,288,758, Food Service at $4,032,399, Troy Career Center at $2,215,068 and Capital Maintenance at $1,885,000.

The 2017-18 appropriations resolution then sets the year ahead:

| Fund | Appropriation |
| --- | --- |
| General Fund | $147,430,144 |
| 2014 Capital Projects Funds | $21,615,000 |
| Debt Service Funds | $18,778,792 |
| Special Revenue Funds | $9,516,614 |
| Capital Maintenance Fund | $1,270,000 |

General Fund revenue is budgeted at $147,458,385 — local $37,990,138, state $97,760,866, federal $3,506,988, incoming transfers and other $8,200,393 — against an estimated July 1, 2017 fund balance of $22,335,432, for $169,793,817 available to appropriate. Instruction takes $101,335,630 (basic programs $83,230,516, added needs $17,245,604, adult and continuing education $859,510). Millage rates: **non-homestead general operating 18.0000, commercial personal property 11.6320, homestead 5.6320, and all properties debt retirement 4.7000.**

**Business — selling Section 11**
The RFP for 18 +/- acres north of Long Lake, east of Rochester Road and west of Allison Street (Sidwell 20-11-328-003 and 20-11-401-001) drew **twelve proposals**, examined with Clark Hill and Great Northern. The recommendation is **Mondrian Properties, L.L.C. at $4,225,000.00** — the same firm that had bid on Section 23 in January and would go on to buy Section 16 and the Section 1 frontage. As with the Section 23 item, the resolution authorizes Dr. Machesky to negotiate and execute a final Offer To Purchase on terms acceptable to him after consulting counsel, rather than approving a completed agreement.

**Business — four service contracts**
Rick West's June 8 memo explains that three contracts expire June 30, 2017.

- **First Student** (buses), initial three-year term from July 1, 2014, extended two years. The reasoning is candid: Troy's per-route cost is very competitive, but "the starting wage for bus drivers is low relative to neighboring districts. This is causing difficulty in staffing" — so the recommendation is a renewal **increasing per-route cost by 5%–8% in the first year and 3%–5% in the second**, citing the nationwide bus driver shortage.
- **Safe-Ed** (security at Athens, Troy High and Troy Career and College High School), a partner since 2011, renewed three years: base contract **$305,000, $310,000 and $315,000** against a current $300,500.
- **Clean-Ed**, six facility maintenance technicians supplementing skilled trades staff, renewed three years at **no additional cost** — Clean-Ed charges a flat fee per employee to handle the HR functions.
- **Sodexo Management, Inc.** food service, renewed for 2017/2018, already approved by the Michigan Department of Education.

**Business — workers' compensation**
The district is self-insured through the State of Michigan with York Risk Management as third-party administrator and Midwest Casualty on excess claims. Claims history has been excellent, which keeps cost low, "however, we do continually have **$400,000 exposure per employee injury**." The Board accepts MASB-SEG's full-coverage proposal effective July 1, 2017 at **not to exceed $98,968.00** — buying a predictable budget number and eliminating that exposure.

**Other — the sinking fund survey**
Epic MRA, the Lansing firm that ran the 2013 bond survey, polled **400 Troy residents** April 20-24, 2017 — registered voters who at least "seldom" vote in local school elections, 20% cell-only, 80% cooperation rate, ±5% at 95% confidence. To keep costs down, a Board member with market research expertise drafted and analyzed it.

The background is stated plainly: the 2013 bond was structured to be tax-neutral, which "also meant it wouldn't cover everything the District knew it needed," and the Board's hope that state funding would recover "hasn't happened." Recent legislative changes broadened permitted sinking fund uses to maintenance, facility improvements and construction, safety and security, and technology. Because the district recently retired debt, a **1-mill sinking fund could be structured with no property tax increase**, yielding **$3.6 million per year for ten years**.

The finding: **61% Yes, 7% leaning Yes, 4% leaning No, 16% No, 12% not sure.** Reasons for Yes run maintenance and upkeep (21%), pro-education or always vote yes (18%), more funding needed (16%), no tax increase (15%), educational quality (5%) and property values (4%). The report's blunt conclusion, repeated across three slides: no tax increase is what earns the endorsement — **"raising it collapses support."** That matters because, as the background notes, a district can pursue only one sinking fund every ten years.

Agenda packet for the regular meeting of the Troy School District Board of Education, June 20, 2017, 7:00 PM at the Services Building, 4420 Livernois, Troy, MI 48098. The agenda is: 1. Pledge of Allegiance; 2. Business — A. Public Hearing: 2017/2018 Proposed Budget; 3. Recognition — A. 2016-2017 School Year in Review, B. Mission Moment: Athens AP Capstone & Seminar Students; 4. Additions & Deletions; 5. Public Communication (agenda items); 6. General – Consent Agenda — A. Treasurer's Report – April & May 2017; 7. Personnel — A. Consideration: Troy Education Association Contract Ratification, B. Consideration: Administrative Appointment – Assistant Principal, Larson Middle School; 8. Curriculum — A. Report: World Language Materials, B. Consideration: World Language Materials Adoption, C. Report: ELD Materials, D. Consideration: ELD Materials Adoption; 9. Business — A. Consideration: 2016/2017 Budget Amendment, B. Consideration: 2017/2018 Budget Appropriations Resolution, C. Consideration: Section 11 Purchase Agreement, D. Consideration: First Student Contract Renewal, E. Consideration: Safe-Ed Contract Renewal, F. Consideration: Clean-Ed Contract Renewal, G. Consideration: Worker's Compensation Insurance, H. Consideration: Food Service Contract Renewal for 2017-2018; 10. Public Communication (non-agenda items); 11. Other — A. Report: Survey Results; 12. Adjournment. Meetings are cablecast on TS-TV Channel 19 (Comcast) and Channel 15 (WOW) every Monday and Wednesday at 2:00 and 9:00 p.m. when school is in session, and viewable at http://vimeo.com/troyschools.

The agenda's ordering is itself notable: business comes before recognition, because item 2.A is the statutory public hearing on the proposed budget, which must precede adoption later in the same meeting.

**Business 2.A: public hearing on the preliminary 2017-2018 budget.** The item attaches a PowerPoint presentation and a draft of the 2017-18 budget book, to be finalized following board adoption of the budget.

**Recognition 3.A: 2016-2017 School Year in Review.** Dr. Rich Machesky, Superintendent of Schools, introduces the video.

**Recognition 3.B: Athens AP Capstone and Seminar students.** Athens AP Seminar teachers Brenda Rice and Sue Syme, along with AP Research teacher Rachel Webb, present a brief overview of the AP Capstone Program. The overview is followed by a question and answer session in which Board members put questions to the students themselves, who answer about their experiences and the unique learning opportunity the program provides. The item records that the students were chosen for the event based on their success in the program and their ability to express themselves well. Athens Principal Lara Dixon introduces the teachers, who in turn introduce their students; the AP Seminar students named include Rija Awan, Nathan Babcock, Saihaj Deol and Rishita Gudeti. Gudeti would appear again eighteen months later among the district's 54 National Merit Scholarship semifinalists.

**Consent agenda 6.A.** The Treasurer's Report for April and May 2017 — two months presented together, as the June meeting is the last of the fiscal year.

**Personnel 7.A: TEA contract ratification.** A tentative agreement between representatives of the Troy Board of Education and the Troy Education Association/MEA/NEA was reached on June 9, 2017. The TEA membership voted to ratify the agreement on June 16, 2017. The tentative agreement is a contract for the period of July 1, 2017 through January 31, 2020, and its specifics are attached, signed by Mr. Tony Lucchi, President of the TEA, and Mr. Jordan Harris, Assistant Superintendent, Employee Services, on June 9, 2017. The resolution ratifies and adopts that agreement.

The timing is tight and deliberate. The Board appointed its negotiating team on February 28, 2017 — Jordan Harris as chief spokesperson with Rick West, Mark Dziatczak, Kris Griffor, Stephanie Trotter and Dave Pass — against a contract expiring June 30. The tentative agreement came on June 9, membership ratification on June 16, and Board ratification on June 20, ten days before expiry. The term chosen is unusual: rather than a clean three-year deal ending June 30, 2020, the contract runs to January 31, 2020, placing the next expiration mid-school-year.

**Personnel 7.B: Assistant Principal, Larson Middle School.** The recommendation is Mr. David Recker. He started his career in education following graduation from college in 2012, teaching language arts and journalism at the Dayton Early College Academy in Dayton, Ohio. He moved to the Troy area in 2014 and accepted a language arts teaching position at Troy High School. During his time in Dayton and at Troy High he fulfilled many additional responsibilities including implementing the International Society for Technology in Education's standards, leading the Continuous Improvement Committee to increase use of best practices, and serving as coordinator for several extracurricular clubs and committees. He holds a bachelor's degree in adolescent to young adult education from the University of Dayton and a Master of Arts in K-12 education administration from Michigan State University. The resolution issues a two-year probationary administrative contract without tenure in the administrative position, effective July 1, 2017. The packet attaches his Oakland Human Resources Consortium online application, submitted May 10, 2017.

**Curriculum 8.A and 8.B: secondary world language materials adoption.** Mark Dziatczak, Deputy Superintendent, and Jennifer Gottlieb, Director of Student Growth, Equity and Accountability, report that Board members reviewed and discussed the recommended world language materials for grades 6-12 for the upcoming school year. The consideration item records that Dziatczak and Gottlieb, along with members of the Teaching and Learning team, provided information on the recommended Chinese, French, German, Japanese and Spanish world language materials for grades 6-12, and that Board members had an opportunity to review textbooks, ask questions and discuss the recommendation at the June 13 Board Workshop. The total cost of these materials is $419,606.82, and the resolution approves them for the 2017-2018 school year in that amount.

**Curriculum 8.C and 8.D: ELD materials adoption.** Mark Dziatczak and Christin Silagy, Director of ELD, Federal Grants and State Assessments, report that Board members reviewed and discussed the recommended ELD materials for grades 6-12. The consideration item records the same June 13 workshop review, gives the total cost of the materials as $171,735.32, and the resolution approves them on the same terms.

The two adoptions together commit close to six hundred thousand dollars of instructional materials in a single meeting, both for grades 6-12, and both reviewed by the Board in person the week before — the packet is careful to record that trustees handled the textbooks themselves.

**Business 9.A: 2016-17 budget amendment resolution.** The amendment covers the General Fund, Debt Service Funds, Food Service Fund, Troy Career Center Fund, Adult Education and Community Service Fund, Facility Rentals Fund, Capital Projects Funds and the Capital Maintenance Fund. The item notes the resolution need not be read in its entirety but must be made part of the official minutes. The amended fund totals include General Fund $146,020,168; Food Service Fund $4,032,399; Troy Career Center Fund $2,215,068; Capital Projects Fund $16,288,758; and Capital Maintenance Fund $1,885,000. This is the year's final true-up, following the Budget Amendment #2 adopted in March.

**Business 9.B: 2017-2018 Budget Appropriations Resolution.** The appropriations resolution covers the General Fund, Special Revenue Funds, Debt Service Funds, Capital Projects Funds and the Capital Maintenance Fund as required by the Department of Education. The resolution approves the general appropriations and budget and millage rates for fiscal year 2017-18 as attached and made part of the official minutes of the June 20, 2017 regular meeting: General Fund $147,430,144; Special Revenue Funds $9,516,614; Debt Service Funds $18,778,792; 2014 Capital Projects Funds $21,615,000; and Capital Maintenance Fund $1,270,000.

The millage rates approved are, by tax base and purpose: non-homestead general operating, 18.0000 mills; commercial personal property general operating, 11.6320 mills; homestead general operating, 5.6320 mills; and all properties debt retirement, 4.7000 mills.

On the revenue side, the General Fund is budgeted at local $37,990,138, state $97,760,866, federal $3,506,988 and incoming transfers and other $8,200,393, for total revenues and incoming transfers of $147,458,385. The estimated fund balance at July 1, 2017 is $22,335,432, all of it available to appropriate, giving total available to appropriate of $169,793,817. Of that, $147,430,144 is appropriated: instruction takes $101,335,630, comprising basic programs $83,230,516, added needs $17,245,604 and adult and continuing education $859,510; support services begin with pupil services at $10,678,738.

The 18 non-homestead mills approved here are the same levy that would be eroded by Headlee and restored by the November 2018 replacement election.

**Business 9.C: Section 11 purchase agreement.** The School District issued a Request For Proposals To Purchase Real Property to obtain proposals to purchase certain surplus vacant real property located in Section 11, and received twelve proposals, examined in conjunction with legal counsel Clark Hill and consultant Great Northern. The recommendation is that the Board authorize the sale of the property to Mondrian Properties, L.L.C. in the amount of $4,225,000.00.

The resolution describes the property as 18 +/- acres of vacant land located north of Long Lake, east of Rochester Road and west of Allison Street in Troy, Michigan, Sidwell Numbers 20-11-328-003 and 20-11-401-001. It recites the proposal from Mondrian Properties, L.L.C. to purchase the property for a purchase price of Four Million Two Hundred Twenty Five Thousand and 00/100 ($4,225,000.00) Dollars; that the district is desirous of authorizing the sale on the terms generally described and substantially similar to those contained in the Purchaser's response and clarifications to the RFP; and that it wishes to authorize Superintendent Dr. Richard Machesky, or his designee, to negotiate the terms and conditions of a final Offer To Purchase on terms acceptable to him after consultation with legal counsel, and to execute the negotiated Offer To Purchase and any documents necessary and incidental to the sale.

This is the sale the March 2017 district-owned property resolution authorized marketing, and it is the largest of the district's land transactions in these packets. The structure is the same one used for Section 23 in January — the Board authorizes a negotiation rather than approving a signed agreement — but unlike the January item, this resolution names the buyer and states the price. Mondrian Properties had first appeared in these packets as one of two bidders discussed at the January 10, 2017 workshop on Section 23; it takes Section 11 here, and would go on to buy Section 16 and the Section 1 front parcel in 2018. Twelve proposals for this parcel is the largest field the district drew for any of its properties.

**Business 9.D through 9.F: service contract renewals.** Rick West's June 8, 2017 memorandum to the Board, copied to Dr. Machesky, explains that the initial terms for three service contracts expire on June 30, 2017 and that the district has been negotiating renewal terms for each.

First Student provides bus transportation services. The initial term was the three-year period commencing July 1, 2014 and ending June 30, 2017, with an option to extend for up to two additional years. West writes that the district currently has a very competitive contract based on per-route pricing and believes it can negotiate a better deal for a two-year renewal than by rebidding the services. His recommendation is candid about the pressure: "Given our competitive per route cost, the starting wage for bus drivers is low relative to neighboring districts. This is causing difficulty in staffing; therefore, we will be recommending a renewal contract that will increase the per route cost by 5% - 8% for the first year and 3% - 5% for the second year." He cites comparative per-route data from other county districts and the nationwide bus driver shortage, and notes the increase will be reflected in the 2017-18 proposed budget. The resolution authorizes administration to finalize the renewal for the 2017/2018 and 2018/2019 school years.

Safe Ed provides professional security consultation solutions at Troy Athens, Troy High School and Troy Career and College High School, under an initial three-year term commencing July 1, 2014. West records that Safe Ed has been a quality partner in providing security services since 2011 and recommends a successor agreement for three years commencing July 1, 2017 and ending June 30, 2020. The current base contract cost is $300,500, and the recommended base contract for the three years is $305,000, $310,000 and $315,000 respectively. The resolution authorizes finalizing the renewal for 2017/2018, 2018/2019 and 2019/2020.

Clean Ed employs six facility maintenance technicians responsible for providing supplemental support to the district's skilled trades staff. The initial term was one year commencing July 1, 2016. West recommends a successor agreement for three years commencing July 1, 2017 and ending June 30, 2020, noting there will be no additional cost for these services as Clean Ed charges a flat fee per employee to handle the human resource functions of employment for these positions.

**Business 9.G: worker's compensation insurance.** The district solicited a worker's compensation insurance proposal from MASB-SEG. It is currently self-insured through the State of Michigan with York Risk Management serving as third-party administrator and Midwest Casualty handling excess insurance claims.

West's June 8, 2017 memorandum explains the trade: "Our claims history has been excellent over the past few years which keeps the cost of our workers compensation low; however, we do continually have $400,000 exposure per employee injury." SET SEG, the district's current property casualty insurance carrier, provides full coverage workers compensation insurance, and given the claims history the district has an opportunity to switch to very affordable full coverage. He recommends making the change, which "will provide us a more predictable budget number for workers compensation and eliminates the $400,000 exposure per employee injury," and notes it would be discussed at the June 13 workshop with the SET SEG proposal attached for review.

The resolution authorizes administration to accept the proposal from MASB-SEG for full coverage worker's compensation insurance effective July 1, 2017 for an amount not to exceed $98,968.00. The item is a clean illustration of what a district buys with insurance: not a lower expected cost — self-insurance with good claims experience is cheap — but the removal of a tail risk and a number the budget can rely on.

**Business 9.H: renewal of food services contract.** On June 21, 2016 the Board approved a resolution allowing administration to enter into a contract with Sodexo Management, Inc. to continue providing the food service operation for the district. The renewal must be approved by the Michigan Department of Education and the Troy Board of Education annually, and the item records that MDE has approved this renewal. The resolution authorizes administration to approve the contract renewal with Sodexo for the 2017/2018 school year.

**Other 11.A: 2017 Sinking Fund Community Input Survey.** The final report, commissioned by the Troy Board of Education and dated June 13, 2017, is organized as introduction, perceptions of district performance, projected sinking fund voting patterns and prevalent public attitudes.

The background section states the problem without hedging. Because of persistent funding gaps from the State, the district continues to seek other ways to fund quality education. In 2013 voters overwhelmingly supported a $125 million bond to help cover many expenses over the bond's 10-year lifespan; the district structured that bond so as not to raise property tax rates, but keeping the bond tax-neutral "also meant it wouldn't cover everything the District knew it needed." The Board hoped state funding would increase sufficiently when the economy improved, "but that hasn't happened." As a result the district continues to struggle to pay for things like preventative maintenance on its buildings. Recent legislative adjustments to appropriate uses for a sinking fund have made it a potential avenue for covering significant district costs such as maintenance, facility improvements and construction, safety and security measures, and technology.

Consequently the Board is considering whether to place a sinking fund proposal on the November ballot. Because the district recently retired some debt, it could structure a new 1-mill sinking fund so that the total school millage rate in Troy would stay where it is, with no property tax increase from what homeowners pay today. That 1 mill would provide the district with $3.6 million per year for the next ten years, to be used to fill current holes in preventative maintenance, update classrooms and technology in a timelier manner, and cover debt payments on new or existing buildings. The report notes the strategic tension: given ongoing needs it would be appropriate to ask for more than 1 mill, "especially because a school district can only pursue one sinking fund every ten years."

Methodology: a phone survey fielded by Epic MRA, a Lansing-based market research company and the firm that completed the 2013 TSD bond survey, averaging 18 minutes in length and fielded April 20 to 24, 2017. To keep district costs as low as possible, a Board member with market research expertise drafted and analyzed the survey following standard research industry practices. The sample was 400 Troy residents living within the Troy School District area, registered voters who indicate they are at least "seldom" voters in local school related elections, with age distribution consistent with voting patterns from the 2011 and 2013 Troy elections. Twenty percent of interviews were completed with cell-only households, and the cooperation rate was extremely high — 80% of those who answered and qualified completed the survey. Full sample results are accurate to within +/- 5% at the 95 percent confidence level. The sample profile is 53% women and 47% men, with an age distribution of 5% aged 18 to 29, 7% aged 30 to 39, 17% aged 40 to 49, 35% aged 50 to 64, 34% aged 65 or older, and 2% declining to say.

The headline finding: the 1-mill sinking fund proposal enjoyed wide support, driven most by a sense of necessity and general educational commitment. On the vote question, 61% said Yes, 7% leaning Yes, 4% leaning No, 16% No and 12% not sure. Reasons given for Yes were maintenance and upkeep important (21%), pro-education or always vote yes (18%), more funding needed (16%), no tax increase (15%), educational quality (5%) and property values (4%).

The report's conclusion is stated three separate times across its slides, in identical words: no tax increase is what earns the endorsement from the community — and raising it collapses support. On the segment analysis, "maybe" voters are characterized as more pragmatic than supporters and less pessimistic than non-supporters, with a conversation around new technology and investment protection identified as the productive line of argument for them.

Read against the strategic tension the background sets out — that a district gets one sinking fund per decade and therefore has reason to ask for more than a mill — the survey's answer is unambiguous: the support is real but it is contingent entirely on tax neutrality, and the district's own polling told it not to reach.

Read as a whole, the June 2017 packet closes the fiscal year and sets up the next several. It ratifies a teacher contract running into 2020, adopts a $147,430,144 General Fund at 18 non-homestead mills, sells eighteen acres for $4,225,000.00 to the developer who would buy two more parcels from the district, locks in four service contracts through 2020, trades a $400,000 per-injury exposure for a $98,968.00 premium, buys nearly six hundred thousand dollars of secondary language materials, and receives the polling that would shape the November ballot question.
